overview.headline: Lift grows with pressure and area, with planform choice shaping coefficients and flap use

keyPoints.point: Lift is directly proportional to area as is the aerodynamic drag force
keyPoints.quote: Like the other aerodynamic force, drag, the lift is directly proportional to the area of the object.

keyPoints.point: Total aerodynamic force equals pressure times surface area around body
keyPoints.quote: The total aerodynamic force is equal to the pressure times the surface area around the body.

keyPoints.point: Lift acts as component perpendicular to flight direction
keyPoints.quote: Lift is the component of this force perpendicular to the flight direction.

keyPoints.point: Designers increase wing area during low velocity takeoff and landing to keep lift high
keyPoints.quote: Takeoff and landing are times of relatively low velocity, so to keep the lift high (to avoid the ground!) designers try to increase the wing area.

keyTerms.gloss: aerodynamic force that depends on pressure variation and area generated by motion through air
keyTerms.quote: The amount of lift generated by an object depends on the size of the object.

keyTerms.gloss: logical reference area generated by wings viewed from above along lift direction
keyTerms.quote: the logical choice is the wing planform area.

keyTerms.gloss: combined top and bottom area proportional to planform reference
keyTerms.quote: We could, in theory, use the total surface area as the reference area.

keyTerms.gloss: experimentally determined value relating lift to area and pressure conditions
keyTerms.quote: Since the lift coefficient is determined experimentally

keyTerms.gloss: movable surfaces sliding backwards to increase wing area for low velocity
keyTerms.quote: This is done by sliding the flaps backwards along metal tracks and shifting the slats forward to increase the wing area.
